0.title: Malachi: The Sun of Righteousness
0.overview:
Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, and it is a conversation with a bored congregation. Nobody here is worshipping idols on the rooftops. The temple has been rebuilt, the services run on time, and the whole thing has gone flat. Serving God, they say, is a weariness (1:13), and they cannot see what they get out of it (3:14).

We know nothing about the prophet except his name, which the ESV notes means "my messenger" — fitting for a book in which messengers keep appearing, and which ends by promising the greatest of them. He wrote after the temple was finished, probably in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah, when the same problems they faced were current: careless priests, mixed marriages, neglected tithes.

The book is built as six disputes. God makes a statement; the people answer back, usually with a question; God replies. But you say is the refrain, and it gives Malachi its distinctive flavour: this is an argument, and God takes their objections seriously enough to answer every one.

God's love (1:2-5). "I have loved you." — "How have you loved us?" He points to his choice of Jacob. God's honour (1:6-2:9). The priests bring blind and lame animals they would never offer the governor, and God says he would rather the temple doors were shut. Faithlessness (2:10-16). Men are discarding the wives of their youth, and God was the witness at those weddings. Justice (2:17-3:5). "Where is the God of justice?" — he is coming, and the question will be who can endure it. Robbery (3:6-12). Withheld tithes, and an invitation to test God's generosity. Profit (3:13-4:3). "It is vain to serve God" — and the promise that the difference will one day be unmistakable.

Two things in this book are easy to misuse, so they need stating plainly. The tithing promise of 3:10 is God's word to a farming nation under the covenant of Moses about rain and harvests; it is not a guarantee that individual givers will get rich, and treating it as one has hurt many people. What it does teach is that God notices what we do with money, that stinginess toward his work is robbery, and that he is extravagantly generous. The New Testament keeps the generosity and changes its spring: God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7). And the passage on divorce (2:13-16) condemns treachery against a faithful wife; it is not a club to beat those whose marriages have already broken, for whom this book's first words and last promise are the answer.

Malachi points to Christ repeatedly. The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (3:1), preceded by a messenger who prepares the way — the verse Mark quotes to open his Gospel of John the Baptist (Mark 1:2). He comes like a refiner's fire to purify rather than merely destroy (3:2-3). And in the final chapter, for those who fear God's name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (4:2), which is what Zechariah sang over the cradle of his son: the sunrise shall visit us from on high (Luke 1:78).

The loveliest verse in the book is easy to miss. While everyone else complained that serving God was pointless, those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him (3:16). God keeps a record of the conversations of ordinary believers who encourage each other in a discouraging time. They will be his treasured possession, spared as a man spares his son who serves him (3:17).

The Old Testament ends with a warning still hanging in the air, and then four hundred years of silence. No prophet spoke. Empires came and went. And then a man appeared in the desert in camel's hair, calling a nation to repent, and behind him came the Lord to his temple. The last word of the Old Testament is "destruction"; the answer to it is a cross, where Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). Malachi's people asked how God had loved them. That is the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — How Have You Loved Us?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: "I have loved you," says the LORD. But you say, "How have you loved us?" (vv. 1-2). God's answer is his choice: Is not Esau Jacob's brother? ... Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated (vv. 2-3). Edom may rebuild, but God will tear down (v. 4), and Israel will say, Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel! (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love for his people rests on his own choice, not on anything in them, and it is visible in their history.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi. "I have loved you," says the LORD. But you say, "How have you loved us?" "Is not Esau Jacob's brother?" declares the LORD. "Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated. I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals of the desert." If Edom says, "We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins," the LORD of hosts says, "They may build, but I will tear down, and they will be called 'the wicked country,' and 'the people with whom the LORD is angry forever.'" Your own eyes shall see this, and you shall say, "Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oracle of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi.

The last book of the Old Testament. The temple has been rebuilt for some decades, the excitement of the return has worn off, and Israel has settled into a dull, disappointed religion. Nobody is worshipping idols on the rooftops any more. They are simply bored with God.

The prophet's name is given (the ESV notes that Malachi means "my messenger"), which fits a book that talks about messengers all the way through, and ends by promising the greatest of them.

The book has an unusual shape. Six times God makes a statement, the people answer back, and God replies to their answer. But you say is the drumbeat of Malachi. It is the record of an argument with a congregation that thinks it has a case.

"I have loved you," says the LORD. But you say, "How have you loved us?" "Is not Esau Jacob's brother?" declares the LORD. "Yet I have loved Jacob

God's opening statement is not a rebuke. It is four words: I have loved you. Everything else in the book stands on that.

And the answer comes back: How have you loved us? Look at the life we are living: a small province, a modest temple, poor harvests, foreign governors. Where is this love?

It is the question of every disappointed believer. Not "is there a God?" but "does he actually love me, given all this?"

God's answer is to take them back before either nation existed, to two brothers in one womb. Is not Esau Jacob's brother? Esau was the elder, with every natural right, and God chose Jacob, the younger, the schemer.

but Esau I have hated. I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals of the desert."

This is hard language, and it must be handled carefully. Paul quotes it: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated (Rom 9:13), and uses it to teach that God's choice does not depend on human merit.

In the Bible the pair "love" and "hate" is often the language of choosing and passing over. Jesus used the same pattern when he said that anyone coming to him must hate his own father and mother, meaning that every other loyalty must come second. God is not describing a spite against Esau the man but the fact that he chose Jacob's line to carry his promise, and did not choose Edom's.

And notice that this is God's evidence for his love. Why are you here at all, complaining about your harvest? Because I chose your father Jacob when there was no reason to.

Christians should hear this personally. If you are in Christ, the answer to "how have you loved me?" is not your circumstances but your election: God set his love on you before you existed, and Christ died for you when you were an enemy.

If Edom says, "We are shattered but we will rebuild the ruins," the LORD of hosts says, "They may build, but I will tear down, and they will be called 'the wicked country,' and 'the people with whom the LORD is angry forever.'"

Your own eyes shall see this, and you shall say, "Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel!"

Edom's determination to rebuild is exactly what Obadiah had confronted, and the verdict is the same. Human resolve cannot outlast God's decision.

And the conclusion Israel is meant to draw is not smugness but worship, and it reaches past their own borders: Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel! God's greatness is not a local matter, which is the theme of verse 11.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Polluted Food on My Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honor? (v. 6). The priests offer polluted food and say the LORD's table may be despised (v. 7): blind, lame and sick animals they would never dare give the governor (vv. 8-9). God would rather the doors were shut than have such worship (v. 10), for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations (v. 11). They find it a weariness (vv. 12-13), and God says, I am a great King (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Worship that costs nothing and gives God the leftovers insults a great King.

verseByVerse.quote: "A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the LORD of hosts to you, O priests, who despise my name. But you say, 'How have we despised your name?' By offering polluted food upon my altar. But you say, 'How have we polluted you?' By saying that the LORD's table may be despised. When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? And when you offer those that are lame or sick, is that not evil? Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? says the LORD of hosts. And now entreat the favor of God, that he may be gracious to us. With such a gift from your hand, will he show favor to any of you? says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear? says the LORD of hosts to you, O priests, who despise my name. But you say, 'How have we despised your name?'

God turns to the clergy, and the argument is simple. Everyone understands that a son honours his father and a servant respects his master. So: where is my honor?

And the priests are genuinely baffled: How have we despised your name? They have not despised it deliberately. That is the point of this whole book. The sins Malachi exposes are not scandals; they are the slow, unnoticed slide of people who still turn up.

By offering polluted food upon my altar. But you say, 'How have we polluted you?' By saying that the LORD's table may be despised.

When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? And when you offer those that are lame or sick, is that not evil? Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? says the LORD of hosts.

Here is the evidence. God's law required unblemished animals (Lev 22:20). The priests were accepting blind, lame and sick beasts: the animals a farmer could not sell, brought to God because they were no use for anything else.

Then the killer question: Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? Try offering the Persian governor a lame sheep as your taxes and see how it goes. They would never insult a human official the way they were insulting God.

The modern version writes itself. We give God the tired end of the day, the money left after everything else, the attention that is left over once the phone has had its share. Nobody decides to do this. It simply happens, and then God asks whether we would treat our employer the same way.

And now entreat the favor of God, that he may be gracious to us. With such a gift from your hand, will he show favor to any of you? says the LORD of hosts.

The sarcasm is heavy. Go on, ask God to bless you, with that in your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain! I have no pleasure in you, says the LORD of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering. For my name will be great among the nations, says the LORD of hosts. But you profane it when you say that the Lord's table is polluted, and its fruit, that is, its food, may be despised. But you say, 'What a weariness this is,' and you snort at it, says the LORD of hosts. You bring what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick, and this you bring as your offering! Shall I accept that from your hand? says the LORD. Cursed be the cheat who has a male in his flock, and vows it, and yet sacrifices to the Lord what is blemished. For I am a great King, says the LORD of hosts, and my name will be feared among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain! I have no pleasure in you, says the LORD of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand.

This is a startling sentence from God. He wishes someone would shut the doors of the temple and stop the services altogether.

Half-hearted worship is not better than no worship; it is worse, because it teaches everyone watching that God is not worth much. God would rather have a locked building than a bored one.

For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering. For my name will be great among the nations, says the LORD of hosts.

And now the horizon opens astonishingly wide. While the priests in Jerusalem are shuffling sick animals onto the altar, God says that his name will be great among the nations from one end of the earth to the other, with a pure offering in every place. (The ESV notes the verbs may be read as present: "is great".)

To a Jew this was almost unthinkable. Worship happened in one place, at one altar, offered by one family. God announces worship in every place, from the nations. Jesus told the woman at the well the same thing: the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth.

There is a sharp rebuke inside the promise. God is saying: if you will not honour me, others will. He is never left without worshippers.

But you profane it when you say that the Lord's table is polluted, and its fruit, that is, its food, may be despised.

But you say, 'What a weariness this is,' and you snort at it, says the LORD of hosts. You bring what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick, and this you bring as your offering! Shall I accept that from your hand? says the LORD.

Here is the heart-condition behind everything: What a weariness this is, and they snort at it. Serving God has become a tiresome job, and they cannot hide their contempt.

That is a devastatingly honest description of how a person can feel about church and prayer, and the honesty is a mercy. God knows when we are bored with him, and it is better to admit it than to perform.

What they brought included animals taken by violence: stolen goods offered to God. It is possible to be generous to God with what was never rightly ours.

Cursed be the cheat who has a male in his flock, and vows it, and yet sacrifices to the Lord what is blemished. For I am a great King, says the LORD of hosts, and my name will be feared among the nations.

The final case is the worst: a man who has a good animal, promises it to God, and then swaps it for a damaged one. Not poverty; deceit.

And the reason this matters is given in six words: I am a great King. That is the answer to every calculation about how little we can get away with giving God. The question is never what we can spare. It is who he is.

And this chapter, which begins with God saying I have loved you, drives us to the one offering that was never blemished. Christ was a lamb without blemish or spot, and he was not the leftover of the flock but the beloved Son.

1.title: I Have Loved You
1.overview:
The oracle of the LORD to Israel by Malachi begins: "I have loved you," and the people answer, "How have you loved us?" God replies with his choice of Jacob over Esau, and with Edom's ruin: they may rebuild, but he will tear down, and Israel will say, "Great is the LORD beyond the border of Israel!" (vv. 1-5).

God then addresses the priests. A son honours his father and a servant his master; where then is his honour? They ask how they have despised his name, and he answers: by offering polluted food on his altar, blind, lame and sick animals they would never present to their governor (vv. 6-9). He wishes someone would shut the temple doors rather than have fire kindled on his altar in vain, for he takes no pleasure in such offerings (v. 10). Yet from the rising of the sun to its setting his name will be great among the nations, with incense and a pure offering in every place (v. 11).

They profane his table, call his service a weariness and snort at it, bringing what has been taken by violence or is lame or sick (vv. 12-13). Cursed is the cheat who vows a good animal and sacrifices a blemished one, for God is a great King whose name will be feared among the nations (v. 14).
1.theology:
God's love for his people rests on his own choice rather than on anything in them (vv. 2-3; Rom 9:13).

The evidence of God's love is not our circumstances but his electing grace (v. 2).

Human determination cannot outlast God's decision (v. 4).

Worship that gives God what we would not dare give an earthly official despises his name (vv. 6-8).

Half-hearted worship is worse than none, because it teaches onlookers that God is not worth much (v. 10).

God will be worshipped by the nations in every place, whether or not his own people honour him (v. 11).

Weariness with God is a real spiritual condition, and God sees it behind the routine (v. 13).

The measure of our giving is not what we can spare but who God is: a great King (v. 14).
1.examples:
A congregation that argues back, six times over.

Two brothers in one womb, and a choice made before either had done anything.

A lame sheep offered to God and never to the tax office.

God wishing someone would lock the church doors.

Incense offered to God in every place on earth, while the temple sulks.

Worshippers snorting at the service.

A man who vows the good animal and swaps in the damaged one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God warns the priests: if they will not give honor to my name, he will curse their blessings (vv. 1-3). His covenant with Levi was one of life and peace, and the model priest walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity (vv. 4-6). For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge ... for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts (v. 7). But these priests have caused many to stumble and shown partiality, so God has made them despised and abased (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who teach God's word are messengers, and when they corrupt it they bring down the people with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O priests, this command is for you. If you will not listen, if you will not take it to heart to give honor to my name, says the LORD of hosts, then I will send the curse upon you and I will curse your blessings. Indeed, I have already cursed them, because you do not lay it to heart. Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and spread dung on your faces, the dung of your offerings, and you shall be taken away with it. So shall you know that I have sent this command to you, that my covenant with Levi may stand, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now, O priests, this command is for you.

If you will not listen, if you will not take it to heart to give honor to my name, says the LORD of hosts, then I will send the curse upon you and I will curse your blessings. Indeed, I have already cursed them, because you do not lay it to heart.

The warning is addressed to the clergy, and the phrase that recurs is take it to heart. Twice God says they will not do it. The problem is not ignorance but inattention; they have heard it all and it has not landed anywhere.

I will curse your blessings is a chilling phrase. The priests' job was to pronounce blessing over the people. God says the blessings themselves will turn.

Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and spread dung on your faces, the dung of your offerings, and you shall be taken away with it.

The language is deliberately disgusting. (The ESV notes offspring is literally "seed".) When an animal was sacrificed, the waste was carried outside the camp and burned. God says he will take that refuse and smear it on the faces of the priests who offered it, and they will be carried out with it.

The point is that what they treated as acceptable worship is, to God, the rubbish from the back of the altar. There is no dignity in ministry done carelessly.

So shall you know that I have sent this command to you, that my covenant with Levi may stand, says the LORD of hosts.

And the aim of even this severe word is restoration: that my covenant with Levi may stand. God is not finished with the priesthood. He is clearing away what has spoiled it.

verseByVerse.quote: My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave them to him. It was a covenant of fear, and he feared me. He stood in awe of my name. True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity. For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. But you have turned aside from the way. You have caused many to stumble by your instruction. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the LORD of hosts, and so I make you despised and abased before all the people, inasmuch as you do not keep my ways but show partiality in your instruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave them to him. It was a covenant of fear, and he feared me. He stood in awe of my name.

Now God describes what a priest was meant to be, and it is a beautiful portrait. The covenant God made with Levi brought life and peace, and it produced a man who feared me and stood in awe of my name. Reverence came first; everything else grew from it.

True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity.

Four marks of a faithful minister of God's word. Measure any teacher against them, including ourselves.

True instruction was in his mouth (the ESV notes this may be rendered "law"): what he taught was accurate. No wrong was found on his lips: he did not shade it to please anyone. He walked with me in peace and uprightness: his life matched his teaching. And he turned many from iniquity: real people actually changed.

For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.

A priest is to guard knowledge, like a man entrusted with something valuable that others need. And notice the title: he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. That is the same word that gives this book its name. Malachi is God's messenger; the priests were meant to be too.

But you have turned aside from the way. You have caused many to stumble by your instruction. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the LORD of hosts,

and so I make you despised and abased before all the people, inasmuch as you do not keep my ways but show partiality in your instruction."

The charge is that their teaching has made many stumble, and that they show partiality: one ruling for the influential, another for the poor. Teaching that bends for important people corrupts everything.

And the result is that the priests are despised by the very people they flattered. Ministers who trim their message to keep people happy lose their respect in the end. Honour cannot be bought with compromise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — The Wife of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Have we not all one Father? Why then are they faithless to one another? (v. 10). Judah has married the daughter of a foreign god (vv. 11-12). They flood the altar with tears and wonder why God does not accept them: because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant (vv. 13-14). God made them one and seeks Godly offspring; so guard yourselves in your spirit (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God is a witness at every wedding, and he takes the breaking of that covenant as seriously as any sin in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why then are we faithless to one another, profaning the covenant of our fathers? Judah has been faithless, and abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem. For Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the LORD, which he loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god. May the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob any descendant of the man who does this, who brings an offering to the LORD of hosts!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Why then are we faithless to one another, profaning the covenant of our fathers?

Malachi turns from the priests to the whole community, and begins with the ground of all human obligation: Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us? Because one God made us, faithlessness to each other is an offence against him.

Judah has been faithless, and abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem. For Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the LORD, which he loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god.

May the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob any descendant of the man who does this, who brings an offering to the LORD of hosts!

The first charge is marriage to the daughter of a foreign god. This is about religion, not race: Israel's law had always welcomed foreigners who came to trust the God of Israel, and Ruth the Moabite is in the Messiah's family tree. The problem is marrying into the worship of another god, which is what Ezra and Nehemiah were dealing with at this time.

And the sting is in the last phrase: the man brings an offering to the LORD of hosts. He keeps coming to church. (The ESV notes the Hebrew of this line is "any who wakes and answers".)

The New Testament instinct is the same: believers are to marry only in the Lord. This is not snobbery about other people; it is realism about what marriage does to the deepest loyalties of a life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this second thing you do. You cover the LORD's altar with tears, with weeping and groaning because he no longer regards the offering or accepts it with favor from your hand. But you say, "Why does he not?" Because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant. Did he not make them one, with a portion of the Spirit in their union? And what was the one God seeking? Godly offspring. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth. "For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence, says the LORD of hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be faithless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this second thing you do. You cover the LORD's altar with tears, with weeping and groaning because he no longer regards the offering or accepts it with favor from your hand.

Now the second charge, and it is the one this chapter is remembered for.

Picture the scene: the altar wet with tears, men weeping and groaning because God will not accept them, and utterly baffled as to why. Emotional worship is not the same as acceptable worship. You can weep at the altar and be in the wrong.

But you say, "Why does he not?" Because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant.

Here is the reason, and it is domestic. God will not hear their worship because of what they have done to their wives.

Three phrases repay attention. The wife of your youth: the woman he married when they were both young, now older, and set aside for someone else. Your companion: a partner and friend, not a possession. Your wife by covenant: marriage is a covenant, not an arrangement, and God was the witness at it.

That is the heart of it. Every wedding has a third party present, whether the couple know it or not.

Did he not make them one, with a portion of the Spirit in their union? And what was the one God seeking? Godly offspring. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth.

(The ESV notes several difficulties in the Hebrew of this verse, and gives an alternative rendering.) The sense is clear enough: God made them one, as Genesis says, and he was seeking Godly offspring, children raised in a home where God is honoured.

Then the command, twice: guard yourselves in your spirit (the ESV notes this may read "take care"). Faithfulness is guarded on the inside, long before anything happens on the outside.

"For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence, says the LORD of hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be faithless."

The ESV notes that this verse is difficult, and gives the older, familiar rendering in its margin: "The LORD, the God of Israel, says that he hates divorce". Either way the message is the same, and it is severe. The man who discards his wife covers his garment with violence: the treachery shows on him like blood on clothing.

A pastoral word is necessary here. Scripture does not treat all divorce identically; Jesus allowed for it in some circumstances, and Paul in another, and the Bible everywhere protects the wronged party rather than trapping them. What Malachi condemns is treachery: breaking a covenant because you have tired of the person you made it with.

And for readers who carry the pain of a broken marriage, whether they were the betrayer or the betrayed, the whole book is the answer. It begins with I have loved you and ends with healing in the wings of the sun of righteousness. God takes covenant-breaking seriously because he takes people seriously, and he is in the business of forgiving and restoring exactly this.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17 — You Have Wearied the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You have wearied the LORD with your words — by saying that evildoers please him, and by asking, Where is the God of justice? (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Cynicism about God's justice wearies him, and his answer is to announce that he is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: You have wearied the LORD with your words. But you say, "How have we wearied him?" By saying, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delights in them." Or by asking, "Where is the God of justice?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have wearied the LORD with your words. But you say, "How have we wearied him?" By saying, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delights in them." Or by asking, "Where is the God of justice?"

The chapter ends with the fifth dispute, and this time the charge is that their talk has wearied God. It is a striking idea. God is never tired, but he can be worn out by a certain kind of conversation.

What wears him out is cynicism. They had been saying two things. First, that God is indifferent to morality: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the LORD. Look around, they said; the crooked prosper and God seems pleased with them. Second, the weary question: Where is the God of justice?

This is the complaint of people who have watched injustice go unpunished for a long time, and it differs from honest lament. Habakkuk asked how long and waited at his watchpost for an answer. These men have stopped expecting one; they are simply grumbling.

And God's answer is the next verse of the book, which happens to be one of the great promises of the Old Testament: Behold, I send my messenger (3:1). They asked where the God of justice was. He replies that he is coming, and that the real question will be who can endure his arrival.

2.title: The Wife of Your Youth
2.overview:
God warns the priests that if they will not take it to heart to honour his name he will curse their blessings, rebuke their offspring and spread the dung of their offerings on their faces, so that his covenant with Levi may stand (vv. 1-4). That covenant was one of life and peace; Levi feared God, true instruction was in his mouth, he walked with God and turned many from iniquity, for a priest's lips should guard knowledge, since he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts (vv. 5-7). But these priests have turned aside, caused many to stumble, corrupted the covenant and shown partiality, so God has made them despised before the people (vv. 8-9).

Have they not all one Father? Why then are they faithless to one another? Judah has profaned the sanctuary and married the daughter of a foreign god (vv. 10-12). They cover the altar with tears, wondering why God does not accept their offerings: because the LORD was witness between each man and the wife of his youth, his companion and wife by covenant, to whom he has been faithless (vv. 13-14). God made them one and was seeking godly offspring, so they must guard themselves in their spirit; the man who divorces treacherously covers his garment with violence (vv. 15-16).

They have wearied the LORD with their words, saying that evildoers are good in his sight, and asking, "Where is the God of justice?" (v. 17).
2.theology:
God's severest words to his ministers aim at restoring, not abolishing, the ministry (v. 4).

A faithful teacher's marks are accurate teaching, integrity, a matching life, and people actually turned from sin (vv. 6-7).

Teaching that shows partiality corrupts the covenant and loses the respect it courted (vv. 8-9).

Because one God created us, faithlessness to each other is an offence against him (v. 10).

Marriage into the worship of another god profanes what God loves; the issue is religious, not racial (v. 11).

Tears at the altar are no substitute for faithfulness at home (v. 13).

Marriage is a covenant at which God himself is the witness, and he seeks godly offspring from it (vv. 14-15; Gen 2:24; Matt 19:6).

Faithfulness is guarded in the spirit, long before anything shows (vv. 15-16).

Cynicism about God's justice wearies him, and his answer is that he is coming (v. 17).
2.examples:
Blessings that turn into curses in the mouths of careless priests.

The refuse from the altar smeared on the faces of those who offered it.

A priest described as a man who guarded knowledge for others.

One ruling for the influential and another for the poor.

An altar wet with tears, and God not listening.

A third party present at every wedding.

Treachery that shows on a man like blood on his coat.

People who ask where the God of justice is and no longer expect an answer.

For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap.<sup>3</sup>He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years.<sup>5</sup>"Then I will draw near to you for judgment. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lord Will Suddenly Come to His Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (v. 1). But who can endure the day of his coming? He is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap (v. 2), who will purify the sons of Levi so that their offerings please God again (vv. 3-4). Then he will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who cheat workers of wages, and those who wrong the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: They asked where the God of justice was; he answers that he is coming, and the question is who can stand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts. But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD. Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years. "Then I will draw near to you for judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against those who swear falsely, against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, against those who thrust aside the sojourner, and do not fear me, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts.

They asked, Where is the God of justice? (2:17). This is the answer, and it is better and more frightening than they expected.

First, a messenger who will prepare the way, like the men who went ahead of a king to clear the road. Four hundred years later a man in camel's hair appeared in the desert, and Mark opened his Gospel by quoting this verse of him (Mark 1:2). Jesus said of John the Baptist, This is he of whom it is written, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face" (Matt 11:10).

Then the one the messenger precedes: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. Notice his temple, and notice that the coming one is the Lord himself. Haggai had promised that the glory of this second temple would surpass the first (Hag 2:9); here is how.

He is also the messenger of the covenant, the one who brings and embodies God's covenant. And there is a gentle irony in in whom you delight: they say they want God to show up. They have no idea what they are asking.

But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap.

Two questions, and both expect the answer "nobody". When God comes, he does not merely arrive; he acts.

Two homely pictures show how. A refiner's fire melts metal to burn off what is mixed into it. Fullers' soap was the harsh lye used by cloth-workers to scour grease out of new wool. Both are violent processes, and both are aimed at cleaning rather than destroying.

He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD.

Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD as in the days of old and as in former years.

Notice the small word sit. A silversmith sits beside the crucible and does not leave it, because metal left too long in the fire is ruined. God gives his full attention to the refining of his people, and he knows exactly how long is enough.

And notice who gets refined first: the sons of Levi, the priests whose corruption filled chapters 1 and 2. God's cleansing starts with the people who handle holy things. (The ESV notes the end of verse 3 may be read "and they will belong to the LORD, bringers of an offering in righteousness".)

"Then I will draw near to you for judgment. I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, against the adulterers, against those who swear falsely, against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, against those who thrust aside the sojourner, and do not fear me, says the LORD of hosts.

Here is the God of justice they had asked for. Read the list slowly. Sorcery and adultery and perjury, yes; and then, in the same breath, those who oppress the hired worker in his wages.

Underpaying an employee stands in Scripture alongside sorcery and adultery. So does wronging the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner. And the root of all of it is the last phrase: and do not fear me.

God will be a swift witness. In a world where such cases never came to court, God says he has seen everything and will testify himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed (v. 6). Return to me, and I will return to you, and they ask, How shall we return? (v. 7). Will man rob God? — in tithes and contributions (vv. 8-9). Bring the full tithe into the storehouse ... and thereby put me to the test, to see whether God will not open heaven's windows (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's unchanging character is why his people survive, and he invites them to test his generosity by being generous.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed. From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my statutes and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts. But you say, 'How shall we return?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed.

One of the great sentences of Scripture, and note the logic of it. God's unchangeableness is not an abstract doctrine here; it is the reason his people are still alive.

If God's love depended on his mood, or on their performance, this generation would have been finished long ago. Because he does not change, the promise made to Jacob still stands over Jacob's descendants, however disappointing they are.

James says the same of God: with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (Jas 1:17). And Hebrews applies it to the Son: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Heb 13:8).

From the days of your fathers you have turned aside from my statutes and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts. But you say, 'How shall we return?'

Return to me, and I will return to you: the same invitation Zechariah had brought to their grandparents (Zech 1:3). God keeps saying it.

And the reply, How shall we return?, can be read two ways. It may be genuine bewilderment, or the defensive shrug of people who cannot think of anything they need to change. Given the tone of the book, the second is likely. God's answer is wonderfully specific: start with your wallet.

verseByVerse.quote: Will man rob God? Yet you are robbing me. But you say, 'How have we robbed you?' In your tithes and contributions. You are cursed with a curse, for you are robbing me, the whole nation of you. Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need. I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your soil, and your vine in the field shall not fail to bear, says the LORD of hosts. Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will man rob God? Yet you are robbing me. But you say, 'How have we robbed you?' In your tithes and contributions.

You are cursed with a curse, for you are robbing me, the whole nation of you.

The question is almost comic: Will man rob God? Who would try? And the answer is: you are doing it, the whole nation of you.

Under the law a tenth of the produce supported the priests and Levites, who had no land, along with the poor. When the tithe stopped, the ministry starved and the poor went without. It was not a technicality; it was theft with victims.

Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house. And thereby put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need.

I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your soil, and your vine in the field shall not fail to bear, says the LORD of hosts.

Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight, says the LORD of hosts.

This is the only place in Scripture where God invites his people to put me to the test. The promise is agricultural: the windows of heaven opened means rain, and the devourer (the ESV notes this is probably a crop-destroying pest) rebuked means harvests that survive.

Two things must be said, because this passage is misused as often as any in the Bible.

First, it is not a formula for personal wealth. God is addressing a farming nation under the covenant of Moses, promising national agricultural blessing for national obedience. To turn it into a guarantee that individual donors will receive money back is to promise something God has not promised here, and it has done real damage to real people.

Second, having said that, do not flinch from what the passage does teach. God notices what we do with money; stinginess toward God's work is robbery; and God is extravagantly generous, until there is no more need. The New Testament does not lower the standard but changes its spring: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7).

The test God offers is not "give and get rich". It is "trust me with your first tenth and see whether I let you down". Generations of Christians have taken him up on it and have no regrets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They have said, It is vain to serve God, and called the arrogant blessed (vv. 13-15). Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him (v. 16). They shall be mine, says the LORD of hosts, in the day when I make up my treasured possession, spared as a man spares his son who serves him (v. 17), and the distinction between the righteous and the wicked will be plain (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: God listens to the conversations of those who fear him and writes them down.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your words have been hard against me, says the LORD. But you say, 'How have we spoken against you?' You have said, 'It is vain to serve God. What is the profit of our keeping his charge or of walking as in mourning before the LORD of hosts? And now we call the arrogant blessed. Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Your words have been hard against me, says the LORD. But you say, 'How have we spoken against you?'

You have said, 'It is vain to serve God. What is the profit of our keeping his charge or of walking as in mourning before the LORD of hosts?

And now we call the arrogant blessed. Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape.'"

The last dispute, and it is the most honest thing they say in the whole book: It is vain to serve God. What is the profit?

They had kept the rules and walked around like mourners, and it had not paid. Meanwhile the arrogant were doing very nicely. It is the complaint of Psalm 73, and of every believer who has watched the unscrupulous prosper.

Notice, though, the assumption buried in the word profit. They served God as an investment, and they are unhappy with the returns. The relationship was commercial all along, which is why God's love in 1:2 meant nothing to them.

There is a searching question here for any Christian who feels God owes them a better life. What exactly did we think we were signing up for? The blessings of serving God are enormous, and most of them are not the ones on this list.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD and esteemed his name. "They shall be mine, says the LORD of hosts, in the day when I make up my treasured possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD and esteemed his name.

And now, in the middle of all this grumbling, one of the loveliest verses in the Old Testament.

While the majority complained, a minority who feared the LORD spoke with one another. We are not told what they said. They were probably encouraging each other to keep going, reminding one another of God's promises, refusing the cynicism around them.

And heaven was listening: The LORD paid attention and heard them. Then this: a book of remembrance was written before him. Kings kept such records of loyal service. God keeps one too, and what he writes down is not great achievements but the conversations of ordinary believers who feared him and esteemed his name.

Two Christians encouraging each other after a discouraging church meeting, a phone call between friends about the goodness of God: that is what goes into the book.

"They shall be mine, says the LORD of hosts, in the day when I make up my treasured possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him.

They shall be mine. The word treasured possession goes back to Sinai, where God called Israel his own treasure out of all the peoples (Exod 19:5). Peter uses the same language of the church (1 Pet 2:9).

And the tenderness of the last line: I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. A father does not treat his working son as a hired hand. God's people are not staff; they are family.

Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.

Their complaint was that there is no visible difference between serving God and not serving him. God does not deny that it looks that way now. He says the day is coming when the distinction will be unmistakable.

That is the answer to every version of this frustration. Wait for the day. And the next chapter describes it.

3.title: Behold, I Send My Messenger
3.overview:
God answers the question "Where is the God of justice?": he will send his messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord whom they seek will suddenly come to his temple (v. 1). But who can endure the day of his coming? He is like a refiner's fire and fullers' soap, sitting to purify the sons of Levi until their offerings please God as in former years (vv. 2-4). He will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who cheat workers of their wages, and those who wrong the widow, the fatherless and the sojourner (v. 5).

Because the LORD does not change, the children of Jacob are not consumed (v. 6). "Return to me, and I will return to you", and they ask how (v. 7). They are robbing God in tithes and contributions, and are cursed with a curse (vv. 8-9). If they bring the full tithe into the storehouse, God invites them to test him: he will open the windows of heaven, rebuke the devourer and make them a land of delight (vv. 10-12).

Their words have been hard against God: it is vain to serve him, and the arrogant prosper (vv. 13-15). But those who feared the LORD spoke with one another; he paid attention and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him (v. 16). They will be his treasured possession, spared as a man spares his son who serves him, and the distinction between the righteous and the wicked will be seen once more (vv. 17-18).
3.theology:
God answers cynicism about his justice by announcing that he is coming himself (v. 1; 2:17).

God's coming is preceded by a messenger, fulfilled in John the Baptist (v. 1; Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10).

God's coming purifies rather than merely destroys, and he sits over the refining with full attention (vv. 2-3).

God's cleansing begins with those who handle holy things (v. 3).

Cheating a worker of his wages stands beside sorcery and adultery in God's list, and the root of all of it is not fearing him (v. 5).

God's unchanging character is the reason his people are not consumed (v. 6; Jas 1:17; Heb 13:8).

Withholding from God's work is robbery with victims, and God invites his people to prove his generosity — which is not a formula for personal wealth (vv. 8-12; 2 Cor 9:7).

Serving God as an investment leads to disappointment with the returns (vv. 13-15).

God listens to the conversations of those who fear him and writes them in a book of remembrance (v. 16).

God's people are his treasured possession and are spared as a father spares his son (v. 17; Exod 19:5; 1 Pet 2:9).
3.examples:
A road crew sent ahead of a king, four hundred years early.

A silversmith who sits by the crucible and does not walk away.

Harsh soap scouring the grease out of new wool.

Unpaid wages listed alongside sorcery and adultery.

The one invitation in Scripture to put God to the test.

People who served God as an investment and are unhappy with the returns.

Two believers encouraging each other, and heaven writing it down.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>"For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch.<sup>2</sup>But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall.<sup>3</sup>And you shall tread down the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>4</sup>"Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rules that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.<sup>6</sup>And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Day Burning Like an Oven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: the day is coming, burning like an oven, when the arrogant and evildoers will be stubble with neither root nor branch (v. 1). But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings, and they will go out leaping like calves from the stall (v. 2), treading down the wicked (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The same day that burns the arrogant rises like sunshine on those who fear God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall. And you shall tread down the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze, says the LORD of hosts, so that it will leave them neither root nor branch.

(In the Hebrew Bible these verses are the end of chapter 3.) Chapter 3 ended with God promising that the difference between the righteous and the wicked would one day be unmistakable. This is that day.

The picture is a clay oven heated white with burning straw. The arrogant — the very people the complainers had called blessed (3:15) — are the stubble that goes in. Neither root nor branch means nothing left to grow again.

The Bible is unembarrassed about this, and love does not require us to be embarrassed either. A world where cruelty and arrogance are never finally dealt with would not be a kinder world.

But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall.

And here is one of the most beautiful sentences in the Old Testament, and the last great promise before four centuries of silence.

The same day that burns like an oven rises like the sun. For you who fear my name, the day of the LORD is not a furnace but a sunrise.

The sun of righteousness: the dawn does not merely announce that night is over; it brings warmth and life with it, and this sunrise brings righteousness. And with healing in its wings, the outstretched rays of the rising sun spreading across the sky like wings, carrying healing with them.

Zechariah the priest, holding his newborn son John, prophesied that the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those in darkness (Luke 1:78). The sun rose in Bethlehem. And every believer who has come out of long spiritual darkness knows what this verse feels like.

Then the response: You shall go out leaping like calves from the stall. Anyone who has seen cattle let out after a winter indoors knows the picture: awkward, delighted, kicking, running for no reason except that they can.

That is God's description of his people on that day. Not a solemn procession: calves let out of the shed.

And you shall tread down the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the LORD of hosts.

The wicked who had seemed untouchable will be ashes. Note the last phrase: on the day when I act. God's people do not bring this about, and they are not told to. They wait.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Remember Moses, and Elijah Is Coming
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember the law of my servant Moses (v. 4). Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes (v. 5), And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The Old Testament closes by pointing back to Moses and forward to the forerunner of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rules that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel. "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rules that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel.

With the Old Testament about to fall silent for four hundred years, God gives two final instructions. The first is: Remember the law of my servant Moses (the ESV notes the last phrase may read "and just decrees").

There will be no prophets for a long time. So hold on to what you already have. That is God's regular provision for his people in quiet seasons: not new revelations but faithful attention to the word he has already given.

"Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.

The second instruction is a promise. Before the great day, God will send Elijah: not necessarily the man himself, but one in his mould, the prophet who confronted a whole nation's idolatry on Mount Carmel.

Four hundred years later, an angel told an old priest that his son would go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah ... to make ready for the Lord a people prepared (Luke 1:17). And Jesus said of John the Baptist, if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come (Matt 11:14), and later, Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him (Matt 17:12).

Most Christians therefore take this promise as fulfilled in John. Some expect in addition a further Elijah-like ministry before Christ's return. All agree that the one whose way was prepared is Jesus Christ.

And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction."

And so the Old Testament ends, and look at where it lands: in the home.

The last work described before the coming of the Lord is not a political revolution or a temple ceremony. It is the hearts of fathers turned to their children, and children's hearts turned back to their fathers. A nation is renewed one household at a time, and a revival that leaves families cold has not gone deep.

The final words are heavy: lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction (the ESV notes this refers to what is devoted to the LORD for destruction). The Old Testament closes on the word "destruction", with a warning still hanging in the air and nothing yet done about it.

Then silence. Four hundred years with no prophet: kingdoms rose and fell, and God's people waited without knowing what they were waiting for.

And then a man appeared in the wilderness in a garment of camel's hair, calling a nation to repent and pointing to someone coming after him. The messenger of Malachi 3:1 had arrived, and behind him came the Lord to his temple, the sun of righteousness rising with healing in his wings.

The curse hanging over the last verse of the Old Testament was not lifted by better behaviour. It fell on him: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). The book that begins with I have loved you and ends with a threatened curse is answered by a cross, and the calves have been let out of the stall ever since.

4.title: The Sun of Righteousness
4.overview:
The day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble set ablaze, with neither root nor branch left (v. 1). But for those who fear God's name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they will go out leaping like calves from the stall (v. 2), treading down the wicked, who will be ashes under their feet on the day when God acts (v. 3).

Remember the law of God's servant Moses, the statutes and rules commanded at Horeb (v. 4). Behold, God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD (v. 5), and he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest God come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction (v. 6).
4.theology:
The final day deals with arrogance and evil completely, and a world in which it never happened would not be kinder (v. 1).

The same day is a furnace to the arrogant and a sunrise to those who fear God's name (vv. 1-2).

Christ is the sun of righteousness who rises with healing, and his coming is the dawn Zechariah sang of (v. 2; Luke 1:78).

The proper picture of God's people in that day is calves let out of the stall (v. 2).

God's people do not bring the day about; they wait for it (v. 3).

In seasons when God seems silent, his provision is faithful attention to the word already given (v. 4).

God prepares the way for his coming by sending a messenger, fulfilled in John the Baptist (v. 5; Matt 11:14; 17:12; Luke 1:17).

The renewal God looks for reaches into the home, turning the hearts of parents and children to each other (v. 6).

The curse that hangs over the last verse of the Old Testament fell on Christ (v. 6; Gal 3:13).
4.examples:
An oven heated white with burning straw.

A sunrise with rays spread out like wings, carrying healing.

Cattle let out of the shed after a long winter.

A final instruction before four centuries of silence: remember what you already have.

A prophet in the mould of Elijah, arriving four hundred years late and exactly on time.

Revival that reaches as far as the kitchen table.

An Old Testament that ends on the word "destruction", and a cross that answers it.
